title: Oman and Iran Issued a Joint Statement in Muscat on 24 June Asserting Joint 'Coastal State' Sovereignty Over Hormuz. The Statement Created a Joint Working Group to Set Future Transit Costs. Rubio, Hours Earlier in the UAE, Said No Country Is 'Allowed to Charge Tolls on an International Waterway.' Ghalibaf Then Said 'Hormuz Will Never Return' to Its Prewar Status
narrative:
On 24 June 2026, the Sultanate of Oman and the Islamic Republic of Iran issued a joint statement from Muscat following a meeting between Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and their Omani counterparts. The statement affirms both countries' 'commitment to the safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, in line with applicable international law,' while simultaneously emphasizing their 'sovereignty and sovereign rights over their territorial waters in the Strait.' The two sides announced a joint working group between their foreign ministries to 'reach agreement on the future administration of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the services that will be provided in this regard and the costs associated with them in accordance with international standards.' Oman separately established a temporary shipping transit corridor in the Strait of Hormuz in coordination with the UN's International Maritime Organisation (IMO), allowing vessels to transit 'without imposing any tolls.'

On the same day, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, speaking at the start of a regional tour in the UAE, rejected the idea of transit fees outright: 'It's an international waterway. No country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway,' adding that he believed 'all the countries in this region would agree.'

Hours later, Ghalibaf, the Iranian Parliament Speaker, told reporters in Oman that 'Hormuz will never return' to its prewar status. The Iranian Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) had published its terms for transiting the strait on 20 June, stating that 'no vessel is permitted to pass through the Strait of Hormuz without a valid passage permit issued by the PGSA.' Iran's permanent representative to the UN in Geneva, Ali Bahreini, said on 23 June that the strait was open for 60 days at no charge, after which 'the future of the strait's access will depend on the outcome of negotiations between Iran and the US.'

analysis:
Three findings structure the 24 June Hormuz diplomatic layer, and each one names a specific evidentiary layer that the prior bilateral US-Iran articles did not contain.

First, the 'two coastal states' formulation in the Muscat joint statement changes the diplomatic geometry from a bilateral US-Iran dispute to a trilateral Oman-Iran-US confrontation over the legal status of the strait. Both Oman and Iran now publicly assert they are the 'Coastal States of the Strait of Hormuz' with sovereignty over territorial waters — the legal foundation under which Iran claims authority to charge for transit services in the future, even after the 60-day waiver. The US position (Rubio: 'It's an international waterway. No country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway') is an on-record contradiction of this joint formulation. No prior Siphoned Truth article contains this bilateral Oman-Iran legal assertion.

Second, the Ghalibaf 'Hormuz will never return' statement is the most aggressive public framing of Iran's intended post-60-day position. The Iranian Parliament Speaker — the second-highest official in the Iranian state after the Supreme Leader — told reporters in Oman on 24 June that the strait 'will never return' to its prewar status. This is structurally incompatible with Rubio's framing of an unchanging international waterway with no tolls. The Pezeshkian 21 June Monetary Conference article treated the toll question as a domestic Iranian messaging question; the 24 June Muscat joint statement escalates it to a documented bilateral escalation with a third party (Oman) co-signing.

Third, the joint working group on 'services' and 'costs' is the institutional foundation for Iran's intended service-fee regime after the 60-day waiver expires. Mostafa Khoshcheshm, a Tehran University professor, told Al Jazeera that 'according to the MoU, Iran is not going to charge service fees for 60 days, but afterwards, Iran is definitely going to do that.' The Muscat statement institutionalizes this intent as a bilateral Omani-Iranian commitment — not just an Iranian domestic-policy aspiration. This is the first time a third country has publicly joined the Iranian framing of post-60-day transit administration.

Fourth, the IMO-coordinated Omani corridor is a parallel governance structure. The Oman's IMO corridor coordinates phased departure dates and waiting areas for vessels — but the corridor was issued by 'the IMO and Omani authorities,' not by Iran's PGSA. Vessels transiting under the Omani IMO corridor do not need a PGSA permit. This is a deliberate architectural choice: Oman is offering an alternative governance path that does not pass through Iran's claimed permit regime. It is also an implicit Omani critique of the PGSA permit framework.

Fifth, Kpler ship-count data confirms the operational reality of the dispute. At least 172 vessels crossed through the Strait since the deal was signed, including 42 ships on Saturday alone — well below the prewar baseline of around 13 crossings per day (averaged over a week, ~91 crossings). More than 250 tankers and 440 cargo ships remain inside the Gulf, with more than 80% of tankers stationary or at anchor and roughly one in six appearing to carry cargo. Jemima Shelley, a senior research analyst at United Against Nuclear Iran, told the BBC that 'we saw tankers passing along the southern corridor at the end of last week and then when Iran declared the strait closed again on Saturday 20 June the transits stalled... there has been some resumption of tankers passing today but still only a trickle.' The 60-day waiver has not restored prewar throughput — and Iran's stated intent is to charge fees after the waiver expires.

Sixth, the 20 June IRGC reclosure of the Strait is the load-bearing structural fact. The IRGC publicly closed the strait on 20 June in response to Israeli strikes on Lebanon — a direct invocation of the cease-fire Article 1 linkage. The strait's reopening is conditional on Israeli compliance with Lebanon terms, not on US-Iran bilateral progress. The PGSA permit regime and the 60-day waiver were both issued AFTER the 20 June IRGC reclosure — they are conditional on the Lebanese ceasefire holding, not on a permanent bilateral settlement. Iran's intended post-60-day service-fee regime is, in effect, an instrument to enforce the Lebanon Article 1 linkage.

The contradiction is structural, not a single statement: the US frames Hormuz as an international waterway with no tolls; Iran and Oman jointly frame it as a bilateral coastal-state administration with future cost recovery; and Ghalibaf's 'will never return' statement is the load-bearing primary source that exposes the gap between the two public positions. The 60-day waiver expires on 22 August 2026.
verdict: The 24 June Muscat joint statement is the first published bilateral Oman-Iran document of its kind: both countries now publicly assert they are the 'Coastal States of the Strait of Hormuz' with sovereignty over territorial waters, and they have institutionalized a joint working group to negotiate 'the services that will be provided... and the costs associated with them' for future transit. This is structurally incompatible with Rubio's on-record position that 'It's an international waterway. No country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway' — and the Ghalibaf 'Hormuz will never return' statement hours later confirms Iran's intended post-60-day direction. The Oman-issued IMO corridor coordinates phasing and waiting areas through 'the IMO and Omani authorities,' not through Iran's PGSA permit regime, creating a parallel governance path that does not pass through Iran's claimed permit authority. The Kpler cumulative count of 172 crossings since the deal was signed — including 42 on Saturday — versus a prewar baseline of roughly 13 crossings per day confirms the dispute is not theoretical: the operational gap between the 'open for 60 days at no charge' framing and the actual ship-count reality is the most concrete measure of how thin the bilateral 'agreement' really is. Beat-distinct from the prior Pezeshkian, Burgenstock, IRGC-Hormuz-closure, and Kpler-toll articles — those are bilateral US-Iran disputes. This is the first published joint Oman-Iran document and introduces a third party (Oman) as a co-administrator with Iran.
